OrthoRef · Foot & Ankle · Hindfoot

Calcaneus Fractures

Mechanism, CT-based classification, timing around the soft tissues, sinus tarsi versus extensile lateral fixation, and the long tail of complications.

Sources: Rockwood & Green’s Fractures in Adults, 10th ed., Ch. 67 · AO Foundation Surgery Reference (marked AO)

IntroductionR&G 67

The calcaneus is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone. About three-quarters of fractures enter the posterior facet of the subtalar joint, and an unreduced or malreduced articular fracture leads to subtalar arthritis — so the goal is an anatomic reduction whenever possible.

65%of tarsal injuries
2%of all skeletal fractures
~75%intra-articular
≤10%open
6–20%spinal injury (mostly lumbar)
3–7.9%bilateral
Who
Young working males
Peak age 20–29. Incidence ~11.5 per 100,000 per year.
Shift with age
Osteoporotic females
Male incidence falls after 60; female incidence rises after 50 with low-energy falls.
Mechanism
Fall from height or MVC
Axial load through the heel. ~20% of fractures are associated with alcohol use.
Burden
Life-altering injury
Patients may be totally incapacitated for up to 3 years and partially impaired for up to 5 years.

Whatever the treatment chosen, the goals are the same: anatomic reduction of the articular surface, restoration of calcaneal height and width, pain-free ambulation, and return to meaningful social and occupational activity.

Historical context — why the pendulum swung
  • Malgaigne described the clinical presentation of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures (DIACF) in 1855.
  • Poor understanding of fracture patterns, suboptimal imaging and inadequate implants made surgical results unpredictable, so nonoperative care was favoured historically.
  • Fluoroscopy, 2D CT, CT-based classifications, better implants and postoperative protocols have since improved surgical outcomes.
  • The extensile lateral approach (ELA) carries a wound dehiscence problem — worse in smokers, diabetics, peripheral vascular disease and open fractures. The sinus tarsi approach (STA) reduced wound and infection problems, but without a thorough grasp of pathoanatomy malreductions have increased.
  • AO Surgery Reference puts calcaneal fractures at approximately 60% of tarsal injuries and bilateral fractures at approximately 10% AO — R&G quotes 65% and 3–7.9% respectively.

Mechanism of injuryR&G 67

The lateral process of the talus is driven like a wedge into the calcaneus by axial load. The tuberosity is driven up while the posterior facet is driven down, concentrating shear across the posterior facet and splitting it into medial and lateral fragments.

Load share
~50% of weight bearing
passes through the calcaneus, with the talus sitting eccentrically medial.
Variables
Pattern is reproducible
Depends on magnitude and direction of force, bony anatomy, foot position at impact and bone quality.
Foot position
Valgus vs varus
A valgus hindfoot places the primary line more laterally; a varus hindfoot places it more medially.

Essex-Lopresti

  • Subtalar joint forced into eversion; the primary fracture line runs across the body at the angle of Gissane, dividing anterior and posterior fragments, then dissipates medially into the sustentaculum.
  • A secondary line from the lateral edge of the talus: force directed posteriorly → joint depression; force directed axially → tongue type (with the counterforce of the Achilles tendon).

Carr

  • Combined shear and compression produce two consistent primary lines: a sagittal line (medial/lateral fragments) and a coronal line starting laterally (anterior/posterior fragments).
  • Continued talar load impacts the posterior facet fragment, displaces it plantarly and rotates it forward into the cancellous-poor "neutral triangle".
  • The sustentacular "constant fragment" rebounds upward, held by its talar attachments; the lateral articular half stays buried and rotated, usually medial to the blown-out lateral wall.

The compression pattern produces an inverted-Y fracture and four typical deformities: loss of height, widening of the heel, varus of the tuberosity, and a lateral wall "blowout".

Associated injuriesR&G 67

Overall
Up to 50%
have another injury; more likely with higher energy.
Spine
~10% lumbar fractures
Maintain a high index of suspicion; image the lumbar spine.
Lower limb
~25% other LE injury
Tibial plateau, pilon, ankle, femur, talar neck and talar fracture-dislocation.

Clinical assessmentR&G 67

Comminution and displacement are proportional to energy and usually track the degree of soft-tissue injury. The soft-tissue findings determine treatment choice and timing.

History
Establish the energy
Height of fall, speed at impact, seat-belt use, alcohol or other substances.
Examine
Open or closed?
Swelling, fracture blisters, at-risk skin, pulses, neurologic status.
Repeat
Serial examinations
In the first hours, to catch compartment syndrome and concomitant injuries.
Sensation
Heel innervation
Branches of posterior tibial, lateral plantar and sural nerves — injury causes later pain and sensory disturbance.

Soft-tissue emergencies and threats

Soft-tissue problemsClassification explorer
Soft tissue
Fracture blisters
  • Appear within 24–48 hours: shear separates epidermis from dermis and the space fills with fluid.
  • Clear (serous) = minimal separation; blood-filled = greater separation, dermis devoid of epidermal cells, more postoperative scarring. Calcaneal fractures produce more blood-filled blisters than other lower-limb trauma.
  • No outcome difference between aspiration, unroofing with silver sulfadiazine, or leaving intact.
  • Incisions through an intact blister or the base of a ruptured one may raise infection risk (evidence inconsistent).
  • Delay surgery until skin integrity returns and the wrinkle test is positive — soft-tissue recovery takes 7–21 days.
Emergency
Calcaneal compartment syndrome
  • Rate after high-energy calcaneal fracture: 10–50%. Irreversible nerve and muscle damage can begin as early as 3 hours.
  • Tense swelling, pain out of proportion, plantar weakness and sensory change, blisters. Severe foot and heel pain is the most consistent symptom; diagnosis is clinical.
  • Late sequelae: claw toes, contractures, motor/sensory dysfunction.
  • Dual dorsal incisions do not reach the calcaneal compartment → a medial plantar approach (from the abductor hallucis origin) is advocated; wounds heal secondarily, with VAC or graft.
  • Release remains controversial; some treat nonoperatively and manage toe contractures with delayed tendon releases.
Emergency
Tongue fracture–associated skin necrosis
  • Tongue-type fractures are ~15% of calcaneal fractures.
  • The Achilles pulls the tuberosity fragment superiorly and dorsally, tenting the posterior heel skin.
  • Seen in up to 21% of tongue-type variants (Gardner).
  • Skin tenting → emergent reduction of the tuberosity fragment and close observation.
High risk
Open calcaneal fractures
  • Up to 10%; 50–90% have associated injuries.
  • Most common wound: transverse medial hindfoot — from a small medial-wall spike puncture to extensive lateral degloving.
  • Transcalcaneal talonavicular dislocation (Ricci): plantarflexed foot on a brake pedal; the talar head may exit the plantar skin.
  • IV antibiotics, tetanus, urgent irrigation and debridement; ex-fix, percutaneous K-wires/Schanz pins, closed reduction or immediate fixation. Repeat debridement every 48–72 hours; early plastic surgery input.
  • Average 2.8 procedures; eventual below-knee amputation 5–8%.

ImagingR&G 67 · AO

Initial films: lateral hindfoot, Harris axial, and Broden views, plus AP/lateral/oblique foot and ankle views. Obtain CT whenever films show intra-articular involvement or suspicion remains.

ViewTechnique / what it shows
Lateral hindfootBest initial view. Confirms fracture, articular depression, joint depression vs tongue type. Shows loss of height, facet depression/rotation, decreased Böhler and increased Gissane angle.
Anterior process lateralBeam directed 20° superior and posterior to the midfoot projects the anterior process clear of the talar neck — the fracture often misdiagnosed as an ankle sprain.
Harris axialHeight loss, increased width, sustentacular rotation, tuberosity angulation. Often too painful acutely.
AP footLeast useful acutely, but shows extension into the CC joint (up to 48%) and subfibular impingement.
BrodenSupine, leg internally rotated 30–40°, beam on the lateral angle at 40°, 30°, 20°, 10° cranial — posterior facet from anterior to posterior. AO describes projections at 30°, 50° and 70° to the horizontal AO.
Ankle mortiseSurrogate Broden view: shows subtalar joint and posterior facet; also useful intraoperatively. Cannot replace CT.

Böhler’s angle: line from the highest point of the anterior process to the highest point of the posterior facet, and from there to the top of the tuberosity. Normal 25–40°, similar to the contralateral side.

A decrease implies facet collapse, but it only changes if the whole facet is depressed and separated from the sustentaculum. If the facet splits into medial and lateral halves you see a double-density sign and Böhler may stay normal. AO: if the angle remains above 15°, nonoperative care can be suggested AO.

Computed tomography

Coronal
Most informative
Posterior facet integrity and alignment, sustentacular position and rotation, tuberosity shape.
Axial
CC joint + sustentaculum
Integrity of the calcaneocuboid joint, parts of the posterior facet and the sustentaculum.
Sagittal
Depression and rotation
Facet depression, rotation, coronal splits; tuberosity and anterior process.
Protocol
3-mm slices
Coronal plane perpendicular to the posterior facet from the lateral scout; axial plane from a second scout (AO: parallel to the sole) AO.
3D-CT and reliability
  • 3D-CT has not significantly improved on 2D-CT.
  • Interobserver reliability for Böhler’s angle was moderate with 2D imaging and fell when 3D was added; reliability for Gissane’s angle rose from slight to fair with 3D.

Outcome measuresR&G 67

No outcome measure is universally applied. Radiographic: articular restoration, Böhler restoration, posttraumatic subtalar arthritis. Patient-reported:

  • VAS
  • SF-36
  • AOFAS Ankle-Hindfoot score
  • Olerud–Molander
  • Foot Function Index
  • Calcaneal Fracture Scoring System
  • PROMIS Physical Function (increasingly used)

Bony anatomyR&G 67

The largest tarsal bone has four articular facets: posterior, middle and anterior superiorly with the talus, and one anteriorly with the cuboid. Most of the bone is porous cancellous bone in a thin cortical shell, and its trabecular architecture shapes the fracture pattern.

Posterior facet
Largest facet
Oval and convex longitudinally, its own joint cavity; sits on the dense "thalamic portion".
Sustentaculum
Carries the middle facet
Supports the talar neck; 2.5 cm below the tip of the medial malleolus; FHL runs in the groove beneath it — at risk from errant screws.
Crucial angle of Gissane
Cortical strut
Thick angled strut from the anterior process to the posterior facet; supports the lateral process of the talus.
Sinus tarsi
Calcaneal sulcus + talus
Palpable depression just anterior and distal to the tip of the lateral malleolus.
Tuberosity
Achilles lever
Achilles inserts into the posterior-inferior two-thirds; inferior surface angled ~30°. Heel pad beneath is immobile and shock-absorbing.
Anterior process
Extra-articular
Most commonly fractured peripheral structure; saddle-shaped CC surface; bifurcate ligament insertion and part of the EDB origin.

The sustentaculum is tethered to the talus by the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament and the deltoid ligament. That is why the sustentacular fragment stays in place — the "constant fragment" — and becomes the anchor to which the articular reconstruction is built.

Soft-tissue relations

Lateral
Peroneal tendons
Run behind the fibula, over the CFL, sheath secured to the peroneal tubercle. Lateral wall comminution can disrupt the CFL insertion and the sheath.
Lateral
Sural nerve + lateral calcaneal artery
Artery runs with the sural nerve midway between fibula and Achilles; supplies the lateral heel skin (the ELA flap).
Medial
Tarsal tunnel
Posterior tibial artery, vein and nerve with the tibialis posterior, FDL and FHL tendons AO.
Protect the lateral calcaneal artery

When extending the sinus tarsi approach proximally, avoid the deep portion of the superior peroneal retinaculum — this protects the lateral calcaneal artery and the blood supply to the lateral heel skin AO.

Pathoanatomy of intra-articular fracturesR&G 67

Intra-articular fractures break into recognizable, recurring fragments. Naming them lets you plan the reduction sequence.

FragmentKey points
Superomedial (A)Sustentacular / constant fragment. Posterior to the primary line, attached to the talus via the deltoid complex. Can rotate into varus, lifting its lateral edge away from the talus.
Superolateral (B)Semilunar / thalamic / comet fragment — lateral posterior facet, on average ~40% of the articular surface.
Tongue (C)Superolateral fragment still attached to the tuberosity and Achilles insertion; secondary line exits below the Achilles.
Anterior main (D)Anterior to the primary line: anterior process plus anterior sustentaculum.
Anterolateral (E)Pyramidal; lateral wall of the anterior process and part of the CC joint.
Posterior main (F)Tuberosity; wedge-shaped, driven up into varus — which pushes the superolateral fragment into valgus and blocks reduction until the tuberosity is repositioned.
Lateral wallThin, usually comminuted; reflected or removed to reach the lateral articular fragment.

PrinciplesR&G 67

No single classification covers all calcaneal fractures. Simpler systems agree more often but guide less; even when surgeons agree on the pattern, they often disagree on the treatment.

Essex-Lopresti (plain radiographs)R&G 67

Joint depression
Facet separate from tuberosity
The articular fragment is fractured free and depressed. Notorious for the degree of joint involvement AO.
Tongue type
Facet attached to tuberosity
Fracture exits posteriorly, splitting the posterior calcaneus in two; needs different reduction and fixation.
Limitations and reliability
  • Interobserver reliability moderate with 2D-CT (κ = 0.50), lower with 3D-CT (κ = 0.33); another study found high intra- and interobserver reliability (κ = 0.85, 0.78).
  • Ability to predict outcome is mixed.
  • The "extra-articular tongue" (Sanders IIC) may have an intra-articular component on CT (IIA/IIB), which changes treatment.

Sanders (CT)R&G 67

Based on the coronal and axial CT of the posterior facet, using the talus as the reference to divide it into lateral, central and medial fragments. The numeral = number of articular fragments; the letter = position of the lines, lateral → medial.

Sanders classificationClassification explorer
Sanders I
Undisplaced
  • All undisplaced fractures, regardless of the number of fracture lines.
  • Expected to do well nonoperatively.
Treatment (R&G)

Nonoperative.

Sanders II
Two-part facet
  • One sagittal fracture line → two main posterior facet fragments.
  • Subtypes IIA, IIB, IIC by line position.
  • AO: 2-part joint injuries are relatively easy to reduce and have a better outcome AO.
Treatment (R&G)

Percutaneous / minimally invasive reduction when needed, or sinus tarsi approach.

Sanders III
Three-part facet
  • Two fracture lines → three fragments; central fragment depressed and rotated.
  • Subtypes IIIAB, IIIAC, IIIBC.
  • A C-line (IIIAC, IIIBC) predicted a worse prognosis.
Treatment (R&G)

Sinus tarsi or extensile lateral approach.

Sanders IV
Four or more parts
  • Three or more lines → four or more fragments; highly comminuted.
  • Needs restoration of calcaneal shape and often a primary fusion.
Treatment (R&G)

Extensile lateral approach ± primary subtalar arthrodesis.

Subtypes
Where the lines fall
  • Letters locate the lines from lateral (A) to medial (C).
  • The more medial the line, the harder the reduction from the lateral side.
  • In the tongue scheme shown in this chapter, IIC is extra-articular (the line runs around and spares the posterior facet), while IIB extends into the facet.
  • Sanders originally used a single slice at the sustentaculum; now multiple slices through the whole facet are reviewed.

Sanders 108 fractures, 10–20 years: type III was 6.5× more likely to develop advanced subtalar arthritis than type II. <20% of type II fractures needed subtalar fusion vs 47.4% of type III.

Sanders reliability
  • Reliability is best at the extremes (simplest and most complex) and weakest for midrange II and III patterns.
  • Interobserver reliability without subclasses was fair (κ = 0.22) and fell to κ = 0.18 with subclasses; intraobserver was moderate (κ = 0.46).
  • Main-type agreement generally exceeds subtype agreement ("moderate" to "substantial").

Other systemsR&G 67 · AO

Zwipp — CT point score (max 12)

Uses lateral and axial calcaneal views, AP foot, Broden, and axial and coronal CT. Points for the number of fragments, number of joints involved, open injury and soft-tissue status; higher score correlated with worse outcome. Interobserver reliability fair (κ = 0.23 plain films, 0.25 2D-CT).

Soeur and Remy (1975) — three degrees
  • First degree: rare; a simple line at the angle of Gissane without articular displacement.
  • Second degree: shear plus compression — line at Gissane with the thalamic fragment compressed into the body.
  • Third degree: comminuted facet "buried near to the plantar cortex". Types II and III are joint-depression variants differing in comminution.
  • Their treatment: open reduction with a small osteotome, pinning the lateral fragment to the sustentaculum, a "rebar" pin under Gissane, and 3 months of plaster.
Müller / AO / OTA

Divides fractures into types A, B and C; the type informs severity, likely outcome and treatment AO.

  • A1 and B2 are extra-articular injuries where surgery is nevertheless indicated AO.
  • C2 has significant joint involvement but is still amenable to successful reconstruction — an anatomic reduction is a must AO.
  • In all types, prognosis improves when calcaneal anatomy is restored AO.

Extra-articular fractures and variantsR&G 67

Extra-articular patternsClassification explorer
Degan & Morrey
Anterior process fracture
  • Avulsion (bifurcate ligament) or compression between cuboid and talus in forced dorsiflexion–eversion; also inversion with a plantarflexed foot.
  • 0.5–10% of foot fractures; age 40–55; more common in women; often misdiagnosed as an ankle sprain. Pain 3–4 cm distal to the lateral malleolus.
  • Associated with CN coalition, ATFL and bifurcate ligament abnormalities.
TypeDescription
INondisplaced avulsion of the tip
IIDisplaced, CC joint spared
IIIDisplaced, involving the CC joint
Treatment

Mostly nonoperative. ORIF if displaced or >25% of the CC articular surface.

Beavis
Tuberosity / beak fracture
  • 1–3% of calcaneal fractures; low-energy fall with forced dorsiflexion and twist, often osteoporotic. Avulsions more common in older women with neuropathy.
  • Type I: small shell of cortex avulsed at the Achilles insertion. Type II (beak): large tuberosity fragment, sometimes reaching the posterior facet.
  • Weak plantarflexion. Soft tissues compromised in ~20%; pale, pressured skin can necrose — worst with delayed treatment or presentation.
Treatment

Closed, displacement <1 cm, skin safe → padded splint in slight equinus with close follow-up. Skin at risk, open, or intra-articular tongue → emergent surgery.

Court-Brown 1986
Fracture-dislocation of the calcaneus
  • Superolateral fragment stays attached to the lateral body; the whole lateral calcaneus is driven up under the fibula, above the lateral process of the talus.
  • With fibular fracture, peroneal subluxation/dislocation, ATFL and CFL injury → tibiotalar instability and varus.
  • Films: talar tilt, lateral malleolar flake fracture (SPR tear), modified double-density sign. CT shows the superiorly displaced facet and varus.
  • Easily missed — a common source of emergency-department litigation.
Treatment

Urgent ORIF — extensile, sinus tarsi, mini-open or percutaneous.

Author’s algorithm for DIACFR&G 67

Two questions drive the decision: open or closed, and for closed injuries, does the skin wrinkle? The answer sets both the timing and the approach.

Sanders I
Splint / boot
Nonweight bearing 6–8 weeks.
Closed · wrinkles
Early STA (1–5 days)
Sanders II and III.
Closed · no wrinkles
Wait (max 21 days) → ELA
Type IV: ELA + subtalar fusion.
Open · small wound
Wash & treat as closed
Small lateral wound away from the incision, or small medial spike wound.
Open · large / degloving
Wash, pin percutaneously
Decide whether ORIF is possible at all; STA/ELA by pattern.

Nonoperative treatmentR&G 67

Indications
  • Nondisplaced intra- or extra-articular fractures
  • Minimally displaced (<1 cm) extra-articular fractures
  • Anterior process fractures with <25% CC joint involvement
Comorbidities favouring nonoperative care
  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Poorly controlled diabetes
  • Heavy smoking
  • Low-functioning household ambulators
  • Medically unfit

Intra-articular (nonoperative protocol)

Day 0
Padded splint, elevation, ice, analgesia
Day 14
Boot or cast, foot in neutral dorsiflexion
2–3 wk
Early ankle ROM, pain and skin permitting
≥6 wk
Nonweight bearing at least 6 weeks, serial films
3 → 6 mo
Low-demand work ~3 months; previous level ~6 months

Extra-articular tuberosity (nonoperative)

Week 1
Padded splint in slight equinus; check skin
7–10 d
Skin intact, no displacement → short-leg cast in slight plantarflexion
6 wk
CAM boot ± heel lift; gentle ankle ROM

Undisplaced or minimally displaced anterior process fractures: short fracture boot with immediate weight bearing and ROM; supportive shoe at 6–8 weeks.

Operative vs nonoperative — evidence

COTS RCT
5.5× more fusion
Nonoperative patients were 5.5 times more likely to need subtalar fusion. Women, younger patients, lighter workloads, non-compensation and better CT reduction did better with surgery.
Meta-analysis
4.4× early fusion
Early subtalar fusion 4.4 times higher after nonoperative care (35 years of literature).
Ägren RCT
Long-term benefit
No better at 1 year, but better long-term despite more complications, because posttraumatic arthritis was reduced.
2022 review
Mixed
Surgery improved shoe fit and return to activity; pain, complications and arthritis did not differ.
Cost
Surgery cheaper overall
Less time off work and lower societal cost with operative care of DIACFs.
Late surgery
~15% subtalar fusion
for posttraumatic arthritis; some need osteotomy or exostectomy for subfibular impingement.

If an anatomic reduction without complications could be reproducibly achieved, there would be no controversy. Sanders cited a learning curve of at least 35 cases; patient selection plus surgical experience best predicts success — an argument for treatment in high-volume centres.

Operative treatment — indications and timingR&G 67 · AO

Extra-articular — fix if
  • Displaced tuberosity (Sanders IIC) or beak fracture
  • Posterior heel skin compromised or at risk
  • Anterior process >25% of the CC surface
  • Compromised gastrocnemius–soleus complex
  • Open extra-articular fracture
Intra-articular — fix if
  • Displaced posterior facet in a medically fit patient
  • Open fracture
  • Fracture-dislocation of the calcaneus
0–2 wk
Percutaneous and STA window; STA ideally within 10 days
2–5 d
Optimal for percutaneous sinus tarsi surgery AO
7–21 d
Soft-tissue recovery; wrinkle test turns positive
2–4 wk
ELA window (plan 14–21 days)
&gt;14 d STA
More wound complications — fragments starting to heal
Timing is the key wound-protection decision

Too early surgery may lead to skin necrosis; observe and protect blisters, and use the return of lateral skin wrinkles as the guide AO.

Extra-articular fixationR&G 67

Displaced tongue-type fracture — percutaneous (Tornetta modification)

Indicated when the tuberosity fragment carries the entire posterior facet, for displaced tuberosity fractures with or without soft-tissue compromise, high soft-tissue risk, medically unfit patients, and fractures <2 weeks old.

Percutaneous tongue reductionStep walkthrough
Position and relax
  • Prone on a radiolucent table; knee flexed ~20°, bump under the ankle for plantarflexion.
  • Thigh tourniquet 325 mm Hg (120 min).
  • Paralysis fully relaxes the gastrocnemius–soleus.
  • Positioning must allow clear lateral, axial and Broden views.
Step 1 / 5
Insert joystick pins
  • Two large (3.2 mm) threaded pins into the superior tuberosity fragment, directed anteroinferiorly down its axis.
  • Do not cross the fracture line yet.
  • Check trajectory and parallelism on the axial or AP view.
Step 2 / 5
Disimpact
  • Plantarflex the foot while pushing the pins down toward the sole.
  • Correct any hindfoot varus at the same time.
  • Confirm anatomic reduction on the lateral view.
Step 3 / 5
Fix
  • Advance a guide pin into the anterior process, stopping short of the CC joint; check lateral, AP and axial.
  • 6.5-mm cannulated screw over it; exchange deformed pins; add a second screw.
  • Supplement with 3.5-mm lag or smaller cortical screws in the tuberosity or thalamic portion.
  • If the line enters the facet, add an STA to see the joint — don’t let tuberosity fixation block articular reduction.
Step 4 / 5
Aftercare
  • Padded splint in mild plantarflexion; regular wound checks. Sutures often stay ≥3 weeks.
  • CAM boot with a 1–2-inch heel lift; gentle ROM.
  • Progressive weight bearing at 5–6 weeks.
Step 5 / 5

Beak (tuberosity avulsion) fractures

  • Prone; small midline incision at the Achilles base ~4 cm above the sole; incise paratenon, debride.
  • Tight Achilles → Strayer gastrocnemius recession through a separate incision.
  • Large pointed clamp; screws may fail against the gastrocnemius pull and thin plantar cortex — add cerclage (Weber technique, Mitchell).
  • Fragment too small for a clamp → suture-bridge fixation with anchors.

Anterior process ORIF

  • Supine or lateral; 3-cm incision just distal to the sinus tarsi in line with the 4th metatarsal; elevate EDB and open the CC capsule.
  • Inspect and irrigate the CC joint; reduce, hold with 1.6-mm K-wires, confirm on an oblique foot view.
  • 3.5-mm cortical screws, or a low-profile mini/small-fragment plate if comminuted; excise small cartilage-free fragments.
  • Sutures out at 3 weeks → CAM boot and ROM; weight bearing at 6 weeks if healing.

Intra-articular fixation — optionsR&G 67

Fracture-dislocation
Lever it back
Small superolateral incision (usually becomes an STA). Identify displaced peroneals; elevator into the subtalar joint ± Schanz pin; lever the fragment inferomedially. Fix the usually two-part sagittal split with 3.5/4.0-mm screws; reduce peroneals, repair SPR and lateral ligaments with anchors. NWB 12 weeks.
Sinus tarsi (STA)
Types II and III, early
Direct view of posterior facet, most of the lateral wall and anterior process; tuberosity reduced percutaneously. Reusable for later arthrodesis. See Approaches.
Extensile lateral (ELA)
Delayed, comminuted, complex
Maximal visualization for anatomic reduction at the cost of wound complications. Needed when fractures cannot be treated early or are highly comminuted.
ORIF + primary fusion
Unreconstructable facet
Severe type III and all type IV, after fixation of the facet fails. Consent beforehand.

ORIF combined with primary subtalar arthrodesis

  • Restore calcaneal shape first (height, width, tuberosity–anterior process–facet relationships) with plates and screws; then judge the joint.
  • Fuse if poorly reduced, severe cartilage delamination, or much of the surface missing.
  • Remove cartilage preserving subchondral bone; perforate the talus with a 2.5-mm drill; graft without overstuffing (throws the hindfoot into varus).
  • One large (6.5–8.0 mm) cannulated lag screw from the heel corner perpendicular to the joint into the talar body; keep as much plate fixation as possible.
  • Serial short-leg casts, NWB 10–12 weeks.
Primary fusion — outcome data
  • Huefner: 6 Sanders IV fractures with ORIF + primary fusion — good or excellent in 5 of 6 at 5 years; all back to work within 9 months.
  • Buckley RCT (ORIF vs ORIF + primary arthrodesis, Sanders IV): small and underpowered; neither group scored well and no difference in SF-36, MFA, AOFAS or VAS.
  • Older patients and those with better restored hindfoot alignment at fusion do better. Potenza: mean AOFAS 85 at midterm.

Heel pad pain after ELA

A silicone heel cup may relieve heel pain from compression injury to the fat pad.

STA vs ELA — outcomesR&G 67

STA advantages
Fewer wound problems
Earlier surgery, shorter operating time, easier closure; better suited to smokers.
STA risks
Not a panacea
Reported loss of reduction; more implant removal; wound complications rise if delayed >14 days; has its own learning curve (Joseph).
Busel
Reduction quality
ELA better for Böhler, facet and tuberosity on CT overall; no difference for Sanders II; ELA trended better for Sanders III.
Kline · Xia
Similar results, fewer wounds
Kline: similar outcomes with fewer wound complications for STA. Xia RCT: shorter surgery, fewer wound complications, higher Maryland scores with STA.
Park RCT (Sanders II)
STA scores better early
Wound complications ELA 12.5% vs STA 0% (NS); STA better VAS/AOFAS at 6 months; ELA restored width better.
Sanders ELA series
97% held reduction
108 fractures, ≥10 years: 71.3% no further surgery, 28.7% late fusion; 80% of type II avoided fusion; 58% of type III needed one.
Surgical pitfalls and preventions (R&G)
SettingPitfallPrevention
PercutaneousFragments underappreciated; inadequate reduction instrumentsStudy cross-sectional imaging, unimpeded fluoroscopy; Schanz/Steinmann pins, K-wires, elevators, distractors, graft
Anterior process ORIFFragment underappreciated; poor CC exposurePlan from CT; reduce under direct vision
STALimited view, cannot convert; complexity underestimated; delayed casesReduction aids and imaging fluency; know its limits; use within 2 weeks and for less complex patterns
Medial approachUnfamiliar anatomyClear understanding and planning
ELALimited by soft-tissue envelopeWrinkle sign present; avoid with microcirculatory compromise
ORIF + fusionLosing height and lengthStructural autograft or allograft available

Choosing an approachR&G 67 · AO

ApproachBest forWatch out for
Percutaneous / MIOTongue-type and tuberosity fractures; high soft-tissue risk; <2 wkNot standardized — incisions follow fracture lines
Sinus tarsiSanders II–III, early (0–2 wk)Limited posterior view; body fragment and primary line not directly seen — needs an adjunct reduction method AO
Extensile lateralComminuted, delayed (2–4 wk), complexApical necrosis, dehiscence up to 25%; needs the wrinkle sign
MedialSustentacular fractures (<10%), medial wall, debriding medial open wounds AONeurovascular bundle; keep the tibiocalcaneal deltoid intact

Sinus tarsi approach (STA)R&G 67 · AO

Through the STA the posterior facet, most of the lateral wall and the anterior process are seen and reduced directly; the tuberosity is reduced percutaneously. AO notes it gives better anterior visualization than the extended lateral approach and similar posterior facet exposure AO.

ORIF via the sinus tarsi approachStep walkthrough
Set-up
  • Supine, bump under the ipsilateral hip, feet flush with the table end (lateral makes a medial approach very hard; prone for bilateral).
  • Thigh tourniquet 325 mm Hg, max 150 min; antibiotics.
  • Kit: Schanz/Steinmann pins, K-wires, small elevators, 2.7/3.5-mm screws and plates, low-profile sinus tarsi plates, graft/cement (rarely), ± 2.7-mm sinuscope.
  • Ideally within 10 days of injury.
Step 1 / 6
Incision
  • 2–5 cm from the tip of the lateral malleolus toward the base of the 4th metatarsal; extend distally for CC involvement.
  • Peroneals lie inferior and posterior; protect them and the sural nerve inferiorly AO.
  • Elevate or split EDB and retract superiorly.
  • Clear fat, debris and haematoma from the sinus tarsi; preserve the interosseous ligament.
  • Intraoperative imaging helps site the incision over the subtalar joint AO.
Step 2 / 6
Reduce the tuberosity
  • Percutaneous Schanz pin: traction and rotation to pull the tuberosity out of varus; confirm on the axial view.
  • Tuberosity blocking? Laminar spreader under the joint fragment (medial wall ↔ tuber body).
  • Unstable joint fragment → back table in saline. Keep lateral wall fragments to restore height.
  • Optional K-wires tuber → constant fragment, kept medial — only if needed, as they limit manipulation.
Step 3 / 6
Reduce the joint
  • Elevate the facet fragments with a small elevator while the tuberosity is held.
  • Removed fragment: 1.6-mm K-wire handle, tip flush with its medial edge.
  • Provisional lateral → medial wires into the sustentaculum; two pins prevent rotation.
  • Check directly and on lateral, Broden and axial views; recheck height, length, width and heel alignment.
  • Subtalar arthroscopy can assist AO.
Step 4 / 6
Fix
  • One or two 2.7/3.5-mm fully threaded cortical screws in lag mode, lateral → sustentaculum.
  • Optional medial approach + one-third tubular buttress plate to pull the tuberosity out of varus.
  • 6.5-mm fully threaded cannulated screws from the tuberosity toward the facet and the anterior process — or a 4.5-mm "kickstand" screw to the subchondral facet.
  • Low-profile sinus tarsi plate slid beneath the facet toward the tuberosity (elevate peroneals first); locking rarely needed.
  • Recheck on lateral, axial and Broden views.
Step 5 / 6
Close
  • Layered closure, minimal handling, Allgöwer–Donati; drains not usually used.
  • Padded below-knee splint; 24 hours of antibiotics.
  • AO: deep layer absorbable; skin subcuticular or interrupted AO.
Step 6 / 6
Modified Kocher extension

A straight STA continued posteriorly crosses the peroneals and sural nerve. A slightly lower incision that can curve around the fibula at the level of the peroneals lets the tendons be moved (not dislocated), shows the CFL and the entire posterior facet to its back edge.

Extensile lateral approach (ELA)R&G 67

Planned at 14–21 days with a positive wrinkle sign. Every step — incision, flap, retraction, closure — is designed to protect the full-thickness flap perfused by the lateral calcaneal artery.

ORIF of joint-depression fracture via ELAStep walkthrough
Position
  • Lateral decubitus on a beanbag, legs scissored: down leg straight, up leg flexed with the heel at the posterior corner.
  • Pad the down leg’s peroneal nerve; pillow between legs; platform under the operative limb.
  • Tourniquet 325 mm Hg, aim to finish within 2.5 hours; re-dose antibiotics after deflation.
  • Read the fracture "personality" on CT beforehand — saves tourniquet time.
Step 1 / 11
Incision
  • Starts ~2 cm above the lateral malleolar tip, 1 cm lateral to the Achilles; vertical limb to the heel, then along the junction of lateral skin and heel pad.
  • The corner is a gentle curve, not a right angle, to avoid apical necrosis; distal limb curves up over the CC joint.
  • Posterior vertical limb keeps dissection deep to the lateral calcaneal artery and sural nerve.
Step 2 / 11
Raise the flap
  • Knife straight to bone, no bevelling; full-thickness subperiosteal flap from the corner.
  • No retractors until ~3 cm is raised; peel the CFL off; see both peroneals or the longus subluxates and is cut.
  • "No-touch" K-wire retractors in the fibula, talar neck and cuboid (± talar body); peroneals subluxated, not dislocated.
Step 3 / 11
Mobilize fragments
  • Benirschke Schanz pin lateral → medial at the posteroinferior tuberosity; pull plantar and into varus to disimpact.
  • Lift the thin lateral wall in one piece (keep it in saline).
  • Get completely under the depressed fragment including dense cancellous bone; disimpact gradually. Remove it to the back table.
  • Broad elevator (or laminar spreader) in the medial line disimpacts the tuberosity from the sustentaculum, restoring height and length.
Step 4 / 11
Clear the path
  • The articular fragment cannot seat if it hits the tuberosity edge — curette, disimpact with more varus, or rongeur blocking bone.
  • Use the talar surface as a template for facet width.
  • Reduce the anterior process first; stretch the interosseous ligament with a spreader — don’t cut it. Disimpact the sustentacular fragment before building to it.
Step 5 / 11
Tongue variant
  • An oblique osteotomy separates the tuberosity from the articular part, converting a tongue into a joint depression pattern.
  • After articular reduction, the oblique cut locks the tuberosity in below the articular block.
Step 6 / 11
Articular reduction
  • Type II: skewer the lateral fragment with two 1.6-mm K-wires, reduce, advance.
  • Type III: build medial → lateral — central to sustentacular (K-wires → 1.5-mm PLLA pins), then lateral.
  • Match anterior and posterior "corners" to the sustentacular fragment — not to the talar undersurface, which over-reduces and forces varus.
  • Valgus on the Schanz pin; anterolateral fragment "clicks" in, restoring Gissane.
Step 7 / 11
Image it
  • True lateral of the talus first.
  • Leg externally rotated 45° and dorsiflexed → mortise/Broden view; tilt the C-arm for front and back of the facet.
  • Foot externally rotated 90°, maximally dorsiflexed, plantar → dorsal beam → axial view.
  • Optional 2.7-mm dry sinuscope for very medial lines; 3D fluoroscopy before screws.
Step 8 / 11
Definitive fixation
  • Facet: 2.7/3.5-mm fully threaded cortical lag screws, aiming slightly plantar and distal to the sustentaculum.
  • The void under the facet is not grafted — the author never had collapse; bone reconstitutes in 1–2 months.
  • Replace the lateral wall; low-profile plate not bent (bending throws the tuberosity into varus). 4.0-mm screws under power.
  • Order: anterosuperior, then posterosuperior and posteroinferior tuberosity holes with thumb pressure and valgus pull. Two screws each into anterior process, tuberosity and facet (Letournel).
  • Locking plate for poor bone: add rafter screws under the facet.
Step 9 / 11
Check the peroneals
  • After removing the K-wires the tendons should drop into the retrofibular groove.
  • Freer in the sheath under the flap to the malleolus and lever forward: firm endpoint = SPR intact; slides anterior to the fibula = SPR torn → repair.
  • More lateral articular lines → more SPR injury. Repair can be done with the tourniquet down.
Step 10 / 11
Close the flap
  • Optional deep drain from the proximal tip of the vertical limb.
  • No. 0 absorbable figure-of-eight deep sutures placed apex → ends, clamped, then tied ends → apex to off-load the apex.
  • Skin: 3-0 monofilament modified Allgöwer–Donati, ends → apex. Dressings, then deflate; bulky dressing and Weber splint.
Step 11 / 11

Medial approachAO

Indication
Sustentaculum and medial wall
Sustentacular fractures are <10% of calcaneal fractures; also helps debride open fractures, most of which occur medially over the sustentacular spike.
Landmark
Two finger breadths below the malleolus
The sustentaculum is palpable there, roughly in line with the medial navicular process.
Incision
~5 cm, centred 2 cm below
Parallels the neurovascular bundle from behind the medial malleolus to the proximal navicular.
Interval
Nerve ↔ FHL
Incise the flexor retinaculum; develop between the posterior tibial nerve and FHL (retracted plantarward). The sustentaculum lies just above FHL.
Protect
Tibiocalcaneal deltoid
Leave it intact — avoids medial instability and preserves deltoid branches to the talar body.

R&G also uses a limited medial approach with a small one-third tubular buttress plate to help pull the tuberosity out of varus during STA fixation (see STA step 5).

OverviewR&G 67

Wound problems dominate after surgery; malunion, impingement and nerve entrapment dominate after nonoperative care of displaced fractures.

up to 25%wound dehiscence
1–4%deep infection (closed)
up to 19%deep infection (open)
~30%symptomatic subtalar arthritis
up to 15%sural nerve injury

Wound complications and osteomyelitisR&G 67

Timing
Up to 4 weeks
The incision closes easily but may dehisce later, most often at the apex (apical wound necrosis).
Risk factors
Host + technique
Smoking, diabetes, open fracture, high BMI and single-layer closure.
Dehiscence
Stop ROM; oral antibiotics; windowed cast with damp-to-dry, or boot + whirlpool
Larger wound
Negative pressure (also usable prophylactically)
Failed
Low-profile fasciocutaneous flap, e.g. lateral arm
Purulence
Admit, serial debridement, culture-specific IV antibiotics ≥6 wk
Diffuse OM
Remove implants and dead bone, antibiotic spacer → later fusion with structural graft

In early, relatively superficial infection (usually superficial osteitis rather than diffuse osteomyelitis), retain the plate and screws until union — typically at least 6 months. Only diffuse osteomyelitis mandates removing all implants. Amputation is rare.

Peroneal tendon problemsR&G 67

Peroneal pathologyClassification explorer
After nonoperative care
Peroneal tenosynovitis and stenosis
  • Expanded lateral wall pushes the tendons against the fibular tip, or dislocates them.
  • After surgery, commoner with the standard Kocher approach (tendons released from the sheath); the ELA largely avoided this — subluxate, don’t dislocate.
  • Adhesions or prominent implants: NSAIDs, physio (mobilization, stretching, eversion strengthening) → tenolysis and/or implant removal.
Joint depression, fracture-dislocation
Peroneal tendon dislocation
  • From lateral wall explosion and shortening, or the tuberosity driven into the talofibular joint.
  • The more lateral the articular line, the greater the chance of SPR injury.
  • Usually recognized intraoperatively at closure; repair by tacking the periosteal sleeve to the posterolateral fibular rim with staples or anchors.
  • Ketz: instability on preoperative imaging 30% vs intraoperative retinaculum testing 11.6%; associated with higher fracture severity, fibular "fleck" sign and fracture-dislocation.

Posttraumatic arthritisR&G 67

Subtalar — radiographic
≈100%
even after anatomic reduction, likely from cartilage injury at impact.
Subtalar — symptomatic
~30%
Fusion rate: Sanders III 47% vs II 19%; type IV higher. Mean time to arthrodesis ~44 months.
SooHoo
3% → 3.49%
subtalar fusion at 1 and 5 years; doubled with open fractures.
Calcaneocuboid
Missed CC extension
or unreduced anterolateral fragment → anterolateral pain. Injection; isolated CC fusion if it fails — residual supination causes lateral column overload.

Secondary subtalar fusion after ORIF is an in situ fusion and does better than reconstruction of a malunion after nonoperative care. Workup of hindfoot pain after ORIF: exclude infection, then diagnostic/therapeutic image-guided injection; conservative measures before open or arthroscopic fusion.

Calcaneal malunionR&G 67

Consequences of a displaced fracture left unreduced:

  • Subtalar and/or CC arthritis from joint incongruity
  • Subfibular impingement from lateral wall expansion and heel widening
  • Peroneal impingement, subluxation or dislocation
  • Loss of height → horizontal talus, anterior ankle impingement, loss of dorsiflexion
  • Hindfoot malalignment altering gait and shoe wear
  • Posterior tibial or sural neuritis
Stephens–Sanders typeFindingsTreatment (via ELA)
ILarge lateral exostosis ± far-lateral subtalar arthrosisLateral wall exostectomy + peroneal tenolysis
IIExostosis + arthrosis across the jointExostectomy + tenolysis + in situ subtalar fusion (local bone graft)
IIIExostosis + severe arthrosis + body malunited in varus/valgusAs type II + calcaneal osteotomy
Malunion — historical techniques and results
  • Cotton (1921): aggressive lateral exostectomy, extra-articular osteotomy, plantar spur resection, forceful subtalar manipulation.
  • Carr: subtalar distraction bone-block arthrodesis with a tricortical iliac graft and 6.5-mm fully threaded screws in non-lag mode; complications included nonunion and varus. Trnka: 41 feet, 5 nonunions, no varus malunions.
  • Romash: osteotomy through the healed primary line, translating the tuberosity under the sustentaculum; 9 of 10 satisfactory.
  • Clare (Stephens–Sanders protocol): union 92.5%, 93.3% neutral or slight valgus, all plantigrade; smoking predicted nonunion and wound problems.
  • Radnay: ORIF → late in situ fusion scored significantly better than malunion reconstruction, with a trend to fewer wound complications.

Other sequelaeR&G 67

Ankle pain
Subtalar stiffness
Inversion–eversion forces shift to the ankle → lateral ankle pain. NSAIDs, brace; arthroscopic debridement for recalcitrant cases.
Heel pad pain
Septal architecture damaged
No effective treatment beyond a heel cushion.
Heel exostoses
Plantar prominences
Heel pads, then excision — avoid a plantar incision (painful scar).
Sural nerve
Up to 15%
Most common neurologic complication (lateral approach). Gabapentin/amitriptyline, inserts; neurolysis or neuroma resection with stump burial.
Nerve entrapment
Posterior tibial nerve
Mostly after nonoperative care — scar, malunited fragment or exostosis. Medial heel pain, worse at night, Tinel positive; confirm by tarsal tunnel injection or EDx → neurolysis.
Compartment sequelae
Claw toes
Contractures and motor/sensory dysfunction after foot compartment syndrome.
